paras: The threatened lynching of A. N. Willey took place at Sunset, Texas, in June 1888, after the physician was accused of stripping and whipping his wife and chasing her through the street with a pistol. Citizens disarmed and held him, and deputy sheriffs took him to the county jail at Montague; dispatches from Gainesville said he was moved "to prevent lynching by the infuriated citizens." The wire story ran nationally; one Ohio paper printed that he was "now being lynched," and several headlines faulted the town for not lynching him.

Sunset was a small town that Gainesville dispatches placed "near here"; its own correspondent called it "our quiet little city." The wire called Dr. A. N. Willey "a prominent physician" and spelled his name Wiley; one paper spelled it Wylie.

According to a special report from Sunset to the Fort Worth Gazette, dated June 9, the town was thrown into "the wildest excitement" the previous evening by news that the doctor was trying to kill his wife. He had stripped and whipped her, and she broke loose and ran down the street screaming for help while he followed with a cocked pistol, warning that he would kill anyone who tried to stop him. The Gainesville wire version added that he fired at her and missed, a detail the Sunset report does not include.

Mrs. Willey ran into a neighbor's house, and citizens, including business men who left their stores open, caught the doctor and took his pistol. A complaint of assault with intent to murder was filed against him in the justice's court, and his examining trial was set for June 9. Deputy sheriffs Norwood and Evans of Bowie arrived about dark and took him to Montague, where he was placed in the county jail.

The Gainesville dispatches said the removal to Montague was made to prevent a lynching by "infuriated citizens." The Sunset report describes the crowd and the prisoner's abuse of those present but makes no mention of a threat to lynch him.

Accounts of Mrs. Willey's injuries differed: the Sunset correspondent wrote that she was badly bruised but "able to be up this morning" and had telegraphed her father to come to her, while the wire said she "will die from the effects of the beating and kicks." No report of her death, of the examining trial, or of any later prosecution of the doctor was found in the coverage.

In Texas, the Fort Worth Gazette printed the Sunset special on June 10 under the headline "Attacked His Wife," and the Austin Weekly Statesman reprinted it on June 14 as "Infamous," with a deck reading "A North Texas Doctor Whips His Wife Nude Through the Streets." A shorter Gainesville dispatch, credited in several papers to the St. Louis Post-Dispatch, ran on June 12 from New York and Savannah to Memphis and was reprinted into late June. Some copies turned the town's name into a time of day, reporting that the beating happened "at sunset."

Headlines played on the nudity, down to the Somerset Herald's "A Modern Godiva." Several papers called for the doctor's death: the St. Paul Daily Globe headed its copy "Should Be Strung Up," and a version carried by Dakota papers ran under "Lynchers Fail in Their Duty," saying the citizens of Gainesville "Criminally Neglect to Give a Brute His Deserts." The Arizona Weekly Enterprise wrote that he "should die also, like a dog upon the end of a rope," and the Middlebury Register in Vermont called him a "monster" who "barely escaped lynching."

Only the Stark County Democrat of Canton, Ohio, reported that he was "now being lynched," a claim no other account supports. Later reprints moved the assault to Sunday, Monday or Tuesday, and none of the papers stated the race of anyone involved.

The date rests on the Sunset report dated June 9, which placed the assault "yesterday evening," or June 8; the Austin Statesman's copy of the same text read "this evening," and the Gainesville wire of June 11 said "yesterday." The Fort Worth Gazette printed its report on June 10, before the wire's implied date, so the local account is the better evidence.

The mob threat also rests on the wire: the Gainesville dispatches said he was jailed to prevent lynching, the Canton paper said he was being lynched, and the Sunset report mentioned only his removal by deputies.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of A. N. Willey
bases: The only collective violence reported is a threatened lynching: wire dispatches say the doctor was jailed at Montague to prevent lynching by infuriated citizens (A2, A13), while the core event was his own assault on his wife (A1).

No one was killed: the local report and most wire copies say he was disarmed and lodged in the Montague jail (A1, A2); the lone 'now being lynched' report (A12) is contradicted by every other account, and the mob threat itself appears only in the wire (A2).
The assault, arrest and jailing at Montague are reported independently by the Sunset special (A1) and the Gainesville wire (A2); the claim of a lynching in progress (A12) stands alone against them.
